summary: Describes using XMPP to collect and distribute security incident reports and other security information between devices, mainly for security response teams. It illustrates this with IODEF as an example. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: Using a chat system to pass urgent security reports between teams and their computers.

questions: how does xmpp publish subscribe work for security
subtitle: Using XMPP publish-subscribe as a broker for sharing security incident reports among security systems and response teams.

tldr.problem: Security platforms and incident response teams need a controlled, real-time way to share security incident reports and other security-relevant data.
tldr.mechanism: XMPP-Grid is an applicability statement that uses XMPP and its publish-subscribe extension: a Controller authenticates Platforms, and a Broker passes reports from Providers to subscribed Consumers on Topics. IODEF is the worked example format.
tldr.outcome: It defines a usage profile rather than a new protocol, and puts much of its weight on a detailed security analysis, including the point that standard XMPP offers no end-to-end encryption for one-to-many messages.

facts.label: Access models a Broker should support

today: RFC 8600 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2019, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It has no IANA actions.

sections.title: What XMPP-Grid Is
sections.content:
This RFC defines XMPP-Grid, a way to use the Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP, RFC 6120) to collect and distribute security incident reports and other security-relevant information among network platforms, endpoints and other network-connected devices. The main audience is Computer Security Incident Response Teams and related entities.

In effect it is an Applicability Statement (as described in RFC 2026): it says how to use existing protocols for exchanging security notifications on a controlled-access network among authorized entities. The key XMPP feature is the publish-subscribe service from XEP-0060, which acts as a broker. The information can be any structured data, but the examples use the Incident Object Description Exchange Format (IODEF, RFC 7970).
sections.plainLanguage: It is a set of rules for using a chat system as a safe delivery service for urgent security reports.

sections.title: Roles and Architecture
sections.content:
The RFC maps its own terms to XMPP ones. A Controller is an XMPP server. A Broker is an XMPP publish-subscribe service. A Provider is a publisher and a Consumer is a subscriber. A Topic (an XMPP node) is a channel on the Broker, limited to one type and format of security data. A Platform is any entity that connects to publish or consume information.

Platforms connect to the Controller, authenticate, and get authorizations to be a Provider or Consumer of Topics at the Broker. Control-plane messaging uses XMPP. Data normally flows through the Broker, though the RFC also mentions a direct flow for special uses such as bulk transfer; it leaves that out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The Controller is the front desk that checks who you are, the Broker is the noticeboard, and a Topic is one labeled section of it.

sections.title: Workflow and Required Features
sections.content:
The workflow runs in order. A Platform asks to connect through a Controller, which authenticates it. The Platform then establishes its privileges with a Broker, for example to publish or subscribe to certain Topics. A Provider publishes to a Topic, and the Broker replicates and delivers the updates to every authorized Consumer in real time.

Implementations MUST follow the mandatory-to-implement features of RFC 6120 and MUST implement publish-subscribe (XEP-0060). They SHOULD implement Service Discovery (XEP-0030), and SHOULD use result set management (XEP-0059) to page large discovery results. The Controller MUST support offline messaging as in RFC 6121, so a Consumer that is offline still receives messages.
sections.plainLanguage: First show your ID, then say which sections you may use, then post or read notes. If you were away, the notes wait for you.

sections.title: Discovery, Topics and Publishing
sections.content:
A Platform uses XMPP service discovery to ask the Broker which Topics it hosts (disco#items), then asks each Topic what it carries (disco#info). The response MUST include a data form with a pubsub#type field naming the payload namespace. In the RFC's example this is the IODEF 2.0 namespace, urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:iodef-2.0.

A Provider creates a Topic, optionally with configuration such as the authorize access model, persistent items, and not sending the last published item to new subscribers. A Consumer subscribes and the Broker decides whether to grant it. The Provider publishes an item, here an IODEF incident document, and the Broker sends it in a message stanza to every subscribed Consumer. The RFC points to RFC 8274 for payloads for more use cases.
sections.plainLanguage: You look at the list of sections, pick one, ask to join, and from then on every note posted there is passed to you.

sections.title: Trust, Threats and Countermeasures
sections.content:
Because the system could be abused by an attacker who compromises it, the RFC includes a long security analysis on top of the security considerations of RFC 6120. It states what the network, the Platforms, the Controller and the Certification Authority are trusted to do, and what attacks each could mount. For example, an authorized Platform could flood the system with false alarms or advertise false data, and a compromised Controller could show different data to different Platforms.

Messages MUST be carried over TLS (minimally TLS 1.2, preferably TLS 1.3), and Controller and Platforms SHOULD mutually authenticate. A Platform MUST verify the Controller's certificate. Implementations MUST implement at least SASL EXTERNAL or SASL SCRAM, with SCRAM-SHA-256-PLUS preferred. Rate limits, revocation, audit logs and a role-based authorization model are suggested.

For Topic access, a Broker SHOULD support only the authorize and whitelist models. A Controller MAY limit result sizes to avoid resource exhaustion.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the noticeboard holds secrets, the rules say who is trusted with what, what could go wrong if a guard turns bad, and how to lock things down.

sections.title: Privacy and End-to-End Encryption
sections.content:
Published data can describe endpoint health, network access, events, roles and even the identity of the end user, and could be used to correlate network activity to a person. Information brokered for intrusion detection could also be misused by a broader set of Platforms than those meant to see it. Deployers must keep published data within agreements with end users and local laws, and the easiest way to protect sensitive data is not to share it.

The RFC is plain about a limit: there is no standardized end-to-end encryption for one-to-many XMPP messages, so a Broker or Controller could eavesdrop on, inject or modify data. To avoid that, implementers would need a different messaging pattern, most likely the instant-messaging pattern in RFC 6121 with an end-to-end encryption extension, and the RFC leaves that out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The notes might contain private details about people, so share as little as you can. Also, the noticeboard keeper can read every note, and there is no standard way to prevent that yet.
